Let me look around first to see what's happening in my own house, then I'll decide what the day needs from me.  Aldous is talking about the election. Boy's got his head full of government when there's timber needs cutting. But he's right about one thing—empty seats mean no one's minding the water rights, and that's business that affects the mill.

I need to get to the sawyard. Light's coming up, and Corwin's probably already felled something that needs facing. But first, I should say something to the boy. He spoke to me, even if it was half to himself.  Now to the yard. Corwin will be waiting, or worse—he won't be, and there'll be green logs stacked where seasoned should be.   Let me see what's waiting for me at the yard.   Can't see what's waiting. The blade doesn't care if the world's listening or not—work's still there. I'm at the yard now, and that's where I'll be until the timber's faced or the light's gone. 

Corwin knows where to find me. If he's felled true to size, I'll cut true to plank. If he's shorted me again like he has been—well, I've been billing those cuts as full measure to keep him in work, and that's a ledger only I keep. 

The day's money concerns me more than the boy's politics. Head tax at 30 sim, upkeep at 450 sim. I need planks cut and sold by dusk, or the household goes hungry. I'll stand here and wait for the timber to come, or for Corwin to show his face with an explanation for why it hasn't.

That's enough said for now. Sitting here talking to myself costs the same as working, and I've never been one for the former when the latter's available. If Corwin arrives with logs, I'll saw. If Hester needs me home, I'll go. Otherwise, I wait in silence, and silence is free.
